name: Vitamin C
summary: Vitamin C is a water-soluble vitamin found mainly in fruit and vegetables. The body can't make it or store much of it, so it needs a steady supply. Shortage over weeks to months causes scurvy, which is rare today but still happens with very limited diets.
roles: Making collagen, the protein that holds skin, gums, blood vessels, bones and wounds together
Helping the body absorb iron from plant foods
An antioxidant that protects cells from damage
Making carnitine (needed to burn fat for energy) and some brain chemicals
Normal working of the immune system

status.note: This app has no vitamin C marker, and it isn't part of routine blood tests. A doctor who suspects scurvy can order plasma vitamin C (ascorbate). EFSA describes below 10 µmol/L as the level where scurvy appears, 10–50 µmol/L as too low with a risk of shortage, and about 50 µmol/L as adequate. The level mostly reflects what was eaten in recent days, falls with infection and inflammation, and the sample has to be handled quickly (vitamin C breaks down in the tube), so a single result has limits.

signs: Tiredness, weakness, low mood and irritability (often the first signs)
Swollen, bleeding gums and loose teeth
Bruising easily; small red-purple spots around hair follicles; corkscrew-shaped hairs
Painful joints and legs, from bleeding into joints and muscles
atRisk: People who eat very little fruit and vegetables, including very selective eaters
Smokers, and people who often breathe others' smoke
Older people who live alone or eat poorly
People on dialysis, and some people with gut diseases that reduce absorption
People with eating disorders or on very restricted diets

signs: Diarrhoea, nausea and stomach cramps at high doses (EFSA noted these at 3–4 g a day)
A higher risk of kidney stones in men who use high-dose supplements, in observational studies
In people with haemochromatosis, extra iron absorption
high.note: Vitamin C from food is not harmful. The body absorbs less as the dose rises, and passes the excess in urine, so very high doses mostly add stomach upset rather than more vitamin C in the body. Part of vitamin C is broken down to oxalate, a main part of most kidney stones, so high doses are a concern for people prone to stones or with kidney disease. Very high doses given by drip (in hospital) can cause red blood cells to break down in people with G6PD deficiency (an inherited enzyme deficiency), and can disturb some lab and finger-prick glucose tests.

examples: Blackcurrants, kiwi fruit, strawberries, oranges and other citrus fruit
Broccoli, Brussels sprouts, kale and cabbage
Tomatoes and potatoes (potatoes add a lot because people eat them often)
foodSources.note: Vitamin C breaks down with heat, light, air and long storage, and leaches into cooking water. Raw, steamed or quickly cooked fruit and vegetables keep more of it.

forms.name: Ascorbic acid
forms.note: The usual form, identical to the vitamin C in food. In human studies synthetic and food vitamin C were absorbed equally well. It is acidic, which some people notice in the stomach.

forms.name: Mineral ascorbates (sodium ascorbate, calcium ascorbate)
forms.note: Vitamin C bound to a mineral, so less acidic. They add sodium or calcium, which matters for people who limit these.

forms.name: Fizzy (effervescent) tablets
forms.note: Often contain a lot of sodium, which matters for people with high blood pressure, heart failure or kidney disease.

forms.name: Slow-release, liposomal, and vitamin C with bioflavonoids
forms.note: Sold as better absorbed, but there is little independent evidence that they make a difference in healthy people. Above about 1 g a day, absorption levels off whatever the form.

forms.name: Ascorbyl palmitate
forms.note: A fat-soluble form used mainly as an additive (to stop fats going off) and in skin creams. There is little data on it as a supplement.

forms.name: Intravenous vitamin C (a drip)
forms.note: Reaches blood levels far above what tablets can. Used in hospital research (for example in sepsis and cancer); it is not a supplement and has its own risks.

reference.noUpperLimit: EFSA found too little data to set a tolerable upper intake level for vitamin C (2004). It noted that up to about 1 g a day from supplements, on top of food, was not linked with stomach or gut problems, while 3–4 g a day can cause them. Absorption levels off at high intakes, so above 1 g a day very little more is taken up and the risk of gut upset rises. There has been no full assessment of the safety of long-term high-dose supplements. The reference intakes are set to keep plasma vitamin C at about 50 µmol/L, with extra for pregnancy (+10 mg) and breastfeeding (+60 mg, to cover vitamin C in breast milk).

interactions.note: Vitamin C increases the absorption of non-haem iron eaten in the same meal. In one trial, adding vitamin C tablets to iron tablets didn't improve results.
Because vitamin C increases iron absorption, vitamin C supplements are usually something to discuss with the doctor treating the condition.
High doses raise oxalate in urine, which can add to stones and, with poor kidney function, build up in the body. Vitamin C supplements are worth discussing with a kidney doctor.

interactions.with: Blood glucose meters and lab tests
interactions.note: Very high doses, mostly given by drip in hospital, can make some finger-prick glucose meters read falsely high or low, and can disturb some lab tests. Ordinary amounts from food or supplements are not known to matter.
Very high doses given by drip can cause red blood cells to break down (haemolysis) in people with this inherited condition.
Whether high-dose antioxidants change how well these treatments work is uncertain; supplements are worth mentioning to the cancer team.
Smokers have lower blood vitamin C and use it up faster. EFSA did not set a separate value for smokers.

cautions: Vitamin C supplements do not prevent colds in everyday life; the small effect is on how long colds last, and only with regular use.
High doses mostly pass out in urine and can upset the stomach.
People with kidney stones, kidney disease or haemochromatosis are best guided by their doctor about vitamin C supplements.

commonUses: May support the body's own collagen production, the protein that holds skin, gums and wounds together.
May help skin look and feel younger by supporting collagen in the skin.
May act as an antioxidant that protects cells from damage by reactive oxygen molecules.
May lower the stress hormone cortisol after stressful events.

origin: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is a water-soluble vitamin that people cannot make themselves, so it has to come from food such as fruit and vegetables. Supplement vitamin C is usually made industrially, often by fermenting glucose from plants such as corn, and is chemically identical to the vitamin C in food.
dosage: The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) sets a population reference intake (PRI) of 110 mg a day for men, 95 mg for women, 105 mg in pregnancy and 155 mg when breastfeeding. EFSA found too little data to set a tolerable upper intake level (the most that is likely safe every day). It noted that up to about 1 g a day from supplements was not linked to stomach or gut problems, while 3 to 4 g a day can cause them. These are population values, not personal targets.
An amount commonly used in studies and supplements is about 500 mg a day. This is not a reference intake or a personal recommendation.

When checking a label, look at the form (ascorbic acid or a mineral ascorbate), how much is in one serving, and whether sodium or calcium is added, for example in fizzy tablets. Absorption levels off at higher doses, so a bigger dose is not taken up in proportion. People with kidney stones, kidney disease or iron overload should check with their doctor.

foodAmounts.verdict: Yes. Fruit and vegetables easily reach the reference intake: about 80 g of raw red pepper or 130 g of kiwi fruit gives 95 mg. The 500 mg amount is also possible but takes a lot of one food, about 400 g of raw red pepper or 250 g of blackcurrants, or a spread of several foods. These are amounts eaten, and cooking and storage lower them.
foodAmounts.notChecked: Food values are from the UK food composition table (McCance and Widdowson's CoFID 2021) built into this app, for the raw food named. Cooked, stored or processed foods contain less.
